questions.stem: By what other name is Fifth Normal Form (5NF) known?
options: Projection–Join Normal Form (PJNF)
Domain–Key Normal Form (DKNF)
Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
Temporal Normal Form
Multi-Valued Normal Form
questions.explanation: 5NF is also known as Projection–Join Normal Form because it concerns redundancy that appears when a table is decomposed into projections and re-joined.

questions.stem: What kind of dependency does Fifth Normal Form address?
options: Functional dependencies
Join dependencies
Partial dependencies
Transitive dependencies
Multi-valued dependencies
questions.explanation: 5NF addresses join dependencies: situations where a table can be reconstructed from multiple smaller tables yet still contains hidden redundancy.

questions.stem: What is the formal condition for a table to be in Fifth Normal Form?
options: It is in BCNF and has no multi-valued dependencies
It is in 3NF and every determinant is a superkey
It is in 4NF and every join dependency is implied by the candidate keys alone
It is in 6NF and every attribute has a validity period
It is in 1NF and every cell is atomic
questions.explanation: A table is in 5NF if it is already in Fourth Normal Form and every join dependency in the table is implied by the candidate keys alone.

questions.stem: In the Fifth Normal Form loan example, into which three binary tables can LoanGuarantorCollateral (LoanID, GuarantorID, CollateralType) be decomposed?
options: Loan, Guarantor and Collateral
LoanAmount, LoanInterestRate and LoanStatus
Customer, Loan and Repayment
LoanGuarantor, LoanCollateral and GuarantorCollateral
LoanID, GuarantorID and CollateralType
questions.explanation: When the three relationships are independent, the ternary table can be derived from LoanGuarantor (LoanID, GuarantorID), LoanCollateral (LoanID, CollateralType) and GuarantorCollateral (GuarantorID, CollateralType).

questions.stem: When should a table be decomposed into its projections under Fifth Normal Form?
options: Whenever the table has more than three columns
Whenever the table has a composite key
Whenever the table stores time-varying attributes
Whenever the table contains a foreign key
When its information equals the natural join of its projections and that dependency is not enforced by keys alone
questions.explanation: If a table's information equals the natural join of two or more of its projections, and that dependency is not enforced by keys alone, the table should be decomposed into those projections.

questions.stem: Which two conditions must a Fifth Normal Form decomposition satisfy?
options: The joined smaller tables recreate the original facts exactly, and no smaller table contains redundant data internally
Every table has a surrogate key, and every attribute has an effective date
The smaller tables share no columns, and each has a single-column key
The decomposition reduces row count, and every table has fewer than three columns
Every constraint is a domain or key constraint, and no joins are required
questions.explanation: The decomposition must recreate the original facts exactly when the smaller tables are joined, and no smaller table may contain redundant data internally.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between Fourth Normal Form and Fifth Normal Form?
options: 4NF applies to warehouses whereas 5NF applies to transactional systems
4NF handles independent multi-valued facts about the same key, whereas 5NF handles redundancy that emerges through join patterns involving three or more attributes
4NF removes transitive dependencies whereas 5NF removes partial dependencies
4NF requires time validity whereas 5NF does not
4NF is theoretical whereas 5NF is used in every schema
questions.explanation: The difference lies in the complexity of dependency: 4NF deals with independent multi-valued facts, while 5NF deals with redundancy that only appears through complex join patterns involving three or more attributes.

questions.stem: In which kinds of domains does Fifth Normal Form become relevant?
options: Simple one-to-many hierarchies
Read-only reporting tables
Highly structured domains with complex many-to-many-to-many relationships where associations are fully independent
Document databases with embedded arrays
Every everyday transactional system
questions.explanation: 5NF is rarely required in everyday transactional systems, but it becomes relevant in highly structured domains involving complex many-to-many-to-many relationships, especially where associations are fully independent.

questions.stem: What should be done if business rules constrain which loan guarantor and collateral combinations are allowed?
options: Decompose to the pure cross-product anyway
Store the combinations as a comma-separated list
Drop the constraint and rely on application logic
Model the constraint with an explicit association table rather than pretending the relationships are independent
Move the constraint into a domain definition
questions.explanation: If business rules block some combinations the relationship is not fully independent, so an extra association table is needed instead of decomposing to a pure cross-product.

questions.stem: Conceptually, what kind of relationships does a table in Fifth Normal Form contain?
options: Only one-to-one relationships
Only relationships with explicit time validity
Only relationships enforced by domain constraints
Only denormalised relationships for query speed
Only irreducible relationships that cannot be further decomposed without losing information
questions.explanation: 5NF ensures that a table contains only irreducible relationships, meaning relationships that cannot be decomposed further without losing information.
